Organization and Description of Business Riot Platforms, Inc. is a vertically integrated digital infrastructure company principally engaged in developing and optimizing its large-scale power assets. The Company’s business strategy centers on enhancing its electrical infrastructure and deploying it across complementary platforms: (i) bitcoin mining and (ii) scalable data center solutions designed to support non-mining workloads. By leveraging its energy portfolio, engineering capabilities, and operational footprint, the Company aims to capitalize on the accelerating demand for power-intensive compute, supported by capital raised through bitcoin production and sales. ​ The Company owns and manages multiple large-scale data center facilities in Texas and Kentucky. The Company provides mission-critical power and infrastructure for Bitcoin Mining at its facilities in Rockdale, Texas (the “Rockdale Facility”), Navarro County, Texas (the “Corsicana Facility”), and its two sites in Kentucky (the “Kentucky Facility,” and together with the Rockdale Facility and the Corsicana Facility, the “Facilities”), and for non-mining Data Center operations at the Rockdale Facility and the Corsicana Facility. The Rockdale Facility currently provides up to approximately 700 megawatts (“MW”) of developed capacity for Bitcoin Mining and data center leasing. The Corsicana Facility is currently equipped to provide up to approximately 400 MW of developed capacity for Bitcoin Mining, and upon completion, is expected to have a total of approximately 1 gigawatt (“GW”) of developed capacity available for high-density compute workloads. The Kentucky Facility currently provides approximately 232 MW of developed capacity. ​ On October 28, 2026, Riot Corsicana, LLC (“Riot Corsicana”), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, entered into a long-term powered land lease agreement (the “Corsicana Lease”) with Anthropic PBC (the “Frontier AI Lab”) to provide critical IT load capacity at the Company’s Corsicana Facility. The Corsicana Lease became effective on November 4, 2026. See Note 3. Data Center Operations . ​ In 2025, the Company began leveraging its core competencies in power optimization, strategic land acquisition, engineering design, and construction execution to develop and monetize portions of its existing facilities and power pipeline through the provision of data center leasing services. During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, the Company entered into long-term data center lease agreements at the Rockdale Facility with Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (“AMD”) for the deployment of 50 MW of critical IT load capacity (the “AMD Lease”), with the potential for additional expansion of up to a total of 200 MW of critical IT load capacity, and with the Frontier AI Lab for the deployment of 191 MW of critical IT load capacity (the “Rockdale Lease”). Bitcoin Mining Industry Consolidation and Emergence of Data Center Alternative The bitcoin mining industry is undergoing significant structural transformation. A combination of factors, including the 2024 halving event, record high network hash rates in 2025, rising mining difficulties, and constrained access to large-scale power resources, has led to increased consolidation across the industry. These dynamics have made efficient, large-scale mining operations increasingly capital-intensive and have prompted miners to seek new avenues for maximizing the value of their existing infrastructure. A notable emerging trend is the convergence of bitcoin mining operations with large-scale data center services, including those supporting AI/HPC workloads. As demand for data center infrastructure accelerates, driven by advances in machine learning, generative AI, and compute-intensive enterprise applications, access to reliable, low-cost power has become a critical constraint on the development of new data centers. Bitcoin mining companies that own and operate their facilities are increasingly repurposing or reallocating portions of their power and physical infrastructure to support data center applications. This shift is enabled by the similarities between 46 Table of Contents the underlying facility requirements for bitcoin mining and data center workloads, including large electrical loads, advanced cooling systems, and high-density rack deployments. ​ As a result, the industry is experiencing an evolution in which mining operators with robust power portfolios are leveraging their existing assets to participate in the rapidly growing market for data center services. This trend reflects both the challenges facing the bitcoin mining sector and the significant economic opportunities presented by the global expansion of compute-intensive digital infrastructure. As the bitcoin mining industry has expanded in recent years, regulatory scrutiny on bitcoin mining facilities and their energy consumption has intensified accordingly. ​ As Texas’s grid operator, ERCOT is responsible for monitoring and testing market participants, including our Bitcoin Mining facilities at the Rockdale Facility and the Corsicana Facility, to evaluate their impact on grid reliability. As part of this process, ERCOT may issue curtailment notices to reduce the power usage at our Texas operations. Our Facilities in Texas are subject to periodic testing and monitoring and have experienced power curtailments in response to instructions we receive from Oncor and ERCOT. Given the inherent uncertainty regarding the duration or extent of power curtailments and testing procedures, we are currently unable to reasonably estimate their potential impact on our operations. If we cannot secure adequate access to electrical power, we may be forced to reduce or shut down our operations. See Part II, Item 1A. “Risk Factors” of this Quarterly Report. ​ Data Center Scrutiny and Regulation ​ Driven by the proliferation of energy-intensive applications such as bitcoin mining and HPC, demand for energy capacity continues to outpace supply. Data centers are increasingly scrutinized by federal, state, and local authorities due to concerns regarding energy 47 Table of Contents consumption, land use, carbon emissions, water usage, environmental impacts, workforce, data-sovereignty considerations, and national-security-related issues. Regulators may impose new permitting requirements, energy-efficiency standards, carbon-reduction mandates, sustainability reporting rules, or operational restrictions specific to data centers, AI infrastructure, or high-density compute environments. Such regulations, particularly at the federal level or in the States of Texas and Kentucky, where our Facilities operate, could increase our capital expenditures, delay development timelines, limit expansion opportunities, or require costly modifications to existing infrastructure. ​ Tax abatement programs that have historically supported development, and specifically, data center development, are subject to increasing scrutiny as residents and policymakers reassess the associated economic benefits to their communities relative to perceived impacts on energy demand, utility costs, and natural resource consumption. In response, certain jurisdictions are becoming more selective in offering incentives or eliminating them altogether. Certain jurisdictions have implemented, or are considering implementing, temporary moratoriums or other restrictions on new data center development due to these concerns. ​ Texas Large Load Regulation ​ Texas legislators, regulators and state officials have recently taken several actions affecting large electrical loads in the ERCOT region, including bitcoin mining and data center facilities. The developments that we currently believe are most relevant to our operations and development plans are summarized below. See also Part II, Item 1A. “Risk Factors” of this Quarterly Report. ​ Interconnection standards. In 2025, the Texas legislature enacted Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”), which, among other things, requires the PUCT and ERCOT to establish new interconnection requirements for large loads. In September 2026, the PUCT adopted final large load interconnection standards implementing SB 6 (PUCT Project No. 58481). The standards apply to new or expanded loads of 75 MW or more at a single site in the ERCOT region and require, among other things, a $100,000 study fee; financial security of $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand (or, upon execution of an interconnection agreement, the greater of that amount and allocated transmission upgrade costs); officer-attested technical disclosures; advance payment of direct interconnection costs; and minimum billing demand commitments. Posted security may be forfeited or applied if a project is withdrawn after transmission capacity is allocated or is not energized within 24 months of its scheduled energization date. ERCOT has also implemented a batch study process, announced in December 2025, under which large load interconnection requests are evaluated together on a portfolio basis. Following the initial study cycle (“Batch Zero”), ERCOT is conducting subsequent study cycles, the rules for which remain under development. The existing capacity at our Rockdale Facility and Corsicana Facility is already interconnected and energized. The additional MWs of capacity planned for the expansion of the Corsicana Facility was studied and approved by ERCOT under its prior large load interconnection process, are not subject to the Batch Zero study process, and are classified as base load. Any new site in Texas, or any other expansion that requires a new or modified interconnection, would be subject to these standards and would be studied in a later batch, which would require us to post financial security before interconnection and could extend our development timelines. ​ Audit and permitting directives. In August 2026, the Governor directed the PUCT and ERCOT to audit data center projects in ERCOT’s Batch Zero interconnection study and to deny interconnection to projects that fail to meet applicable requirements. On August 20, 2026, the PUCT granted ERCOT’s request for good cause exceptions to Batch Zero deadlines to allow time to complete the audit, which has delayed the Batch Zero study and the resulting capacity allocations. ERCOT expects to complete the audit in or around December 2026. Because the existing capacity at our Rockdale Facility and Corsicana Facility was already energized, it is not subject to the audit. On September 21, 2026, the Governor further directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (“TCEQ”) to suspend the issuance of permits sought by data center projects pending completion of the audit and the Texas Water Development Board’s evaluation of the impact of data centers on municipal water supplies. ​ Water-use reporting. Texas officials have intensified enforcement of the Texas Water Development Board’s mandatory water-use survey requirements, and the Texas Office of the Attorney General (“OAG”) has opened an investigation into data center compliance with those requirements. We have completed the survey in each of the past two years and, to our knowledge, the investigation does not currently include the counties in which we operate. ​ Transmission cost allocation and curtailment. SB 6 requires the PUCT to amend its wholesale transmission cost-allocation rules by December 31, 2026. The PUCT is considering measures that could require large loads to bear a greater share of transmission upgrade costs, pay minimum demand charges based on contracted peak demand for a period of 20 years, and replace the current four coincident peak (“4CP”) cost-allocation methodology with a twelve coincident peak (“12CP”) methodology. Our participation in ERCOT’s 4CP Program reduces the transmission charges on our power bills in the following year. See “Strategic Goals and Initiatives—Power Strategy” above for further information. If the PUCT adopts a 12CP methodology, we expect our transmission-related charges to increase and the benefit of our 4CP-avoidance strategy to decline, which could increase our all-in power cost at 48 Table of Contents our Texas facilities. SB 6 also requires ERCOT to ensure that utilities serving customers interconnected after December 31, 2025 develop protocols, including the installation of any necessary equipment before interconnection, to enable the curtailment of those loads during firm load-shed events. Because our existing Texas facilities were interconnected before that date, we believe these requirements should not apply to them; however, we may be subject to curtailment in the future pursuant to Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits (“IROLs”) if we are unable to utilize equipment that is sufficiently effective at enhancing grid reliability. ​ Grid stability requirements. ERCOT’s voltage and frequency ride-through requirements for large computational loads (Nodal Operating Guide Revision Request 282 and Nodal Protocol Revision Request 1308) became effective on August 1, 2026. These requirements establish frequency and voltage ride-through standards for certain large loads, subject to an exemption for loads that were operational, or had received ERCOT’s written approval to energize (or had signed an interconnection agreement, completed the required interconnection studies, posted required financial security, and provided the notice to proceed), on or before November 14, 2025. Our existing operations at the Rockdale Facility and Corsicana Facility qualify for this exemption. Expansion capacity that does not qualify for the exemption may require modifications to cooling equipment and associated electrical systems, and ERCOT is considering a separate NOGRR addressing cooling loads. ​ In addition, ERCOT, working with transmission service providers, manages the grid to stay within IROLs, which are system limits that, if exceeded, could lead to instability or cascading outages. Because large loads that are exempt from the ride-through requirements may trip offline during grid disturbances, ERCOT has grouped these loads by region, including in North and Central Texas, and established IROLs and mitigation plans for each group. Once a group’s aggregate consumption approaches its limit, ERCOT will activate a mitigation plan, after which each transmission service provider must keep its affected loads at or below an assigned “not to exceed” limit. Our Corsicana Facility is included in an IROL group, and its consumption could be capped or curtailed as other loads in the group increase their consumption, even if our own usage does not change. As of the date of this Quarterly Report, ERCOT has not activated a mitigation plan for this group. ​ See Part I, Item 1A. “Risk Factors” of the 2025 Annual Report and Part II, Item 1A. “Risk Factors” of this Quarterly Report for additional discussion regarding potential impacts that our competitive and evolving industry may have on our business. ​ Recent Events Affecting the Company Global supply chain disruptions and inflationary pressures have, at times, resulted in delays to our miner delivery schedules, infrastructure development timelines, and the manufacturing and delivery schedules within our Engineering segment.
